claims.text: Dash Platform is a layer-2 Web3 technology stack on top of Dash: a decentralized data storage and application layer where developers define schemas and submit structured state transitions instead of deploying arbitrary user-written code on-chain.

Its two core components are Drive (consensus-verified decentralized storage of user-created data) and DAPI (a decentralized HTTP API exposing JSON-RPC and gRPC endpoints covering both Core layer 1 and Platform layer 2).

Application data is stored in Drive and held in GroveDB, an authenticated hierarchical store that returns cryptographic proofs with query responses, so a client does not have to trust the API provider that its data is authentic.

To store data, a developer first registers a data contract — a JSON-Schema description of the application's document types (their fields, types, and indexes) — analogous to defining a schema for a document-oriented database like MongoDB.

A document is the atomic unit of stored user data (resembling a document in a document-oriented DB); every document must comply with its app's data contract and carries base fields such as $id, $type, $dataContractId, $ownerId, $revision, and timestamps.

Writes arrive as state transitions — a versioned header, a payload, and the authoring identity's signature — covering operations such as data-contract creation, document and token updates, identity management, credit transfers, and masternode voting.

Identities are the foundational user primitive: one or more public keys recorded on the platform chain that control a user's profile and sign their documents, plus a credit balance established by locking Dash on layer 1.

Credits are the fee mechanism: locking Dash on the Core chain creates credit balance that pays the state-transition fees of platform activity, and credits can convert back to Dash subject to a daily network limit.
DPNS registers human-readable .dash names tied to an identity and is itself implemented as an application built on top of Platform.
Developers can create and manage fungible tokens (comparable to ERC-20 style assets) without writing smart contracts, using data contracts, token state transitions, and access-control groups.
NFTs are supported as Platform documents: each has a unique id, can be immutable or mutable and deletable, supports ownership change, and has a built-in transfer-and-purchase system.
DashPay is a data-contract application providing a user-centric wallet where payments are addressed by username through encrypted contact-request channels.
The docs' end-to-end example apps are Dashnote (a notes app exercising the document CRUD lifecycle) and DashMint Lab (an NFT marketplace); DashPay is the flagship data-contract wallet.

The curriculum's remaining hands-on modules (4 through 18) are: environment setup / verified read, fund a Platform address, create a Dash identity, register a DPNS username, data contracts, write a data contract, documents, submit a document, query documents, document transfer and purchase, tokens, and token-paid document creation.
Taken together, modules 4-18 compose one small end-to-end testnet application that touches DAPI, identities, names, data contracts, documents, and tokens.

Module 2 scope: must cover 'how Platform stores application data', 'concrete things you can build', and 'what you will build in this course'; must not cover masternode quorums and LLMQs, InstantSend-versus-ChainLock mechanics, Tenderdash/consensus internals, or re-teaching what a blockchain is.

uncertainties.topic: Payment-confirmation speed belongs to module 1, not module 2
uncertainties.resolution: Payment speed is acknowledged only in passing via 'Core settles Dash payments' — the money-layer contrast — and is never given its own section or quiz item, so module 2 does not duplicate module 1's mustCover.

uncertainties.topic: Avoiding the hard mustNotCover boundary 're-teaching what a blockchain is'
uncertainties.resolution: The lesson opens with a single-sentence bridge that assumes module 1 ('you met Dash the money'), and never re-defines a blockchain, a block, or consensus.

uncertainties.topic: How much of the Core/Platform split to restate
uncertainties.resolution: The split is restated in a two-bullet list plus a one-way-relationship sentence, focused solely on the data-storage contrast, so the lesson stays within its 12-minute budget.
